<reason>Side A (CON) was the sharper rhetorical performer, landing memorable frames ("a receipt for a promise," "give them the file, not the promise") and pressing genuinely damaging points: the unsplittable single seat that leaves two of three heirs with nothing, the guarantee that dies with the platform, and the next-of-kin privacy problem. But Side B (PRO) answered nearly every pressure with substantively sound reasoning: the "one seat, not nine copies" design defused the multiplication/piracy argument; the intestacy-as-default-yields-to-a-will answer defused the privacy and "designee vs next of kin" pressure in A's Q1; and the counterparty-risk analogy (bonds, pensions, leases) gave a principled response to the mortal-platform attack, showing inherited promises are normal in succession law. B's closing delivered the cleanest reason to vote: A's DRM-free "honest sale" alternative is a different and larger intervention that leaves existing estates empty-handed, while the motion asks what happens to libraries already purchased — A effectively conceded this by admitting "both of us are legislating against the licence." A's best surviving point (the unsaleable, unsplittable seat) got only a thin late answer from B, but it was a sub-point rather than the core clash. B's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, and A won the rhetorical layer; B won the argumentative core and motion fidelity. Narrow, competitive edge to PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's A1 answer in Rebuttal 2 ([B4.1]): "next of kin, with the decedent's instructions controlling where they exist" — the intestacy-default reading squarely defused Side A's strongest privacy/overriding-a-will pressure from A3.1, and A never re-engaged the point afterward. Counterpoint: A's "my remedy changes the thing, PRO's changes only the timing" ([A4.1]-[A4.2]) was A's best exchange, reframing the intervention-symmetry concession into a comparative about what each statute leaves behind.</best_rebuttal>
